intro: Rachmaninoff’s Polka de V.R. is a piano piece built on a polka his father liked to play, with the tune kept over a dance bass and more elaborate figuration added around it. This recording was made by the composer for Edison in 1919.

sections.label: A · Allegretto, tune over polka bass
sections.mNote: Allegretto; bass notes alternate with light chords.

sections.label: B · Poco più mosso, staccato chords
sections.mNote: Poco più mosso; both hands play accented chords.

sections.label: C · Meno mosso, slurred melody
sections.mNote: Meno mosso; a slurred melody over left-hand chords.

sections.label: D · Scherzando, four sharps
sections.mNote: Tempo precedente; the key signature changes to four sharps.

sections.label: A′ · A♭ tune, Tempo I
sections.mNote: Tempo I; the opening dance returns with a countermelody.

sections.label: Coda · Meno mosso, ritardando, final pp chord
sections.mNote: Meno mosso, ritardando, closing on a pp chord.

cues.title: Entry of the polka tune
cues.text: A few bars of semiquavers slow down and get softer before the tune enters at pp. The left hand alternates a bass note with a chord, the oom-pah of the polka. Above it, the right hand plays small triplets between the melody notes.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 1: Allegretto, diminuendo and ritardando before the pp tune and alternating bass notes and chords. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/polka-de-w-r.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Behr’s polka, arranged 1911
cues.text: Vasily Rachmaninoff liked to play this tune, and his son gave the arrangement his father’s initials. The melody is Franz Behr’s Lachtäubchen, a Scherzpolka, Op. 303, also known as La rieuse. Rachmaninoff moved it from F to A♭ major and dedicated his 1911 version to Leopold Godowsky.
cues.evidence: Jeremy Nicholas’s notes for Hyperion identify the polka Vasily played as Behr’s Scherzpolka, Op. 303, and give the transposition from F major to A♭, the 1911 arrangement and the Godowsky dedication: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5662_GBAJY9148612. IMSLP’s page for Behr’s Op. 303 lists the titles La rieuse (polka badine), Lachtäubchen, Scherzpolka and Laughing dove Polka: https://imslp.org/wiki/La_rieuse,_Op.303_(Behr,_Franz).

cues.title: Meno mosso episode
cues.text: Meno mosso slows the dance after the staccato chords. A slurred melody moves over left-hand chords. A tempo restores the pace, and a second Meno mosso slows it again.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, pp. 3–4: ritardando, Meno mosso and repeated alternations with a tempo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Edison recordings, April 1919
cues.text: In April 1919 Rachmaninoff, newly arrived in America and in need of money, agreed to record for Edison. Edison wanted ten sides at once, before any contract was signed, and issued all three takes of each. The RCA booklet to the reissue describes the sound as “distant and disappointing”.
cues.evidence: RCA/BMG booklet to the 10-CD Complete Recordings (09026 61265 2, 1992), essay “The Recordings”, p. 28: the April 1919 Edison contract, the ten sides, three takes of each all issued, and the phrase “distant and disappointing”. https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992

cues.title: Change to four sharps
cues.text: At the double bar the key signature changes from four flats to four sharps. The marking is Tempo precedente, with scherzando written above the first chord. Accented chords and sixteenth-note figures follow in both hands.
cues.evidence: Boston Music Co. edition (1919), Internet Archive item polkaonthemebywr00rach: the four-sharp signature at the double bar ending printed p. 5, and “Tempo precedente” and “scherzando” above the first bar of p. 6, with accented chords and sixteenth-note figures; the signature returns to four flats on p. 6 before “Tempo I”. https://archive.org/details/polkaonthemebywr00rach
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the main theme, A♭ major
cues.text: A♭ major returns at Tempo I. Rachmaninoff adds a countermelody of his own to Behr’s tune, while the bass keeps the same accompaniment pattern as before.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 5, Tempo I and continuation; Jeremy Nicholas’s Hyperion notes identify the new countermelody accompanying the main theme’s return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars, Meno mosso
cues.text: A pp run rises through the upper register. Meno mosso and a ritardando slow the final bars, and the piece ends on a soft chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 8, final system: pp rising run, Meno mosso, ritardando and final pp chord with fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Short chords in both hands
transitions.from: A · Allegretto, tune over polka bass
transitions.to: B · Poco più mosso, staccato chords
transitions.how: At Poco più mosso the tempo quickens. In A♭ major both hands play short, accented chords. The dynamic starts at mf and rises through f to ff. Rests separate the pairs of chords, and the bass continues to leap.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3: Poco più mosso, staccato chords, crescendo, f and ff.

transitions.title: Descending run into Meno mosso
transitions.from: B · Poco più mosso, staccato chords
transitions.how: A descending right-hand figure and a ritardando lead away from the ff chords. At Meno mosso the right hand plays a slurred melody above moving inner notes and a held left-hand chord, and the marking drops to mf.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3, final two systems: descending figure, ritardando and Meno mosso at mf.

transitions.title: Veloce run leads to four sharps
transitions.how: Poco a poco rallentando slows the melody. A run marked veloce begins pp, grows louder and descends, and the left hand stops beneath its last notes. At the double bar the key signature changes to four sharps. Tempo precedente restores the earlier tempo, and scherzando is written above the melody.
transitions.evidence: Boston Music Co. edition (1919), Internet Archive item polkaonthemebywr00rach, printed pp. 5–6: poco a poco rallentando, the veloce run marked pp, the four-sharp signature at the double bar, Tempo precedente and scherzando.

transitions.title: Return to four flats and Tempo I
transitions.how: At the end of the four-sharp passage the key signature changes back to four flats. The right hand plays forte sextuplets above broken chords in the left hand, and a ritardando leads into Tempo I. The A♭ major tune returns at p with a second melodic line beside it.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 5: four-flat signature, forte sextuplets, ritardando and Tempo I; the added countermelody is discussed in Jeremy Nicholas’s Hyperion notes.

transitions.title: Meno mosso and the final chord
transitions.to: Coda · Meno mosso, ritardando, final pp chord
transitions.how: A long pp run rises across the keyboard before Meno mosso. The left hand holds a low octave and the right-hand line slows through a ritardando. A final high chord at pp, under a fermata, ends the piece in A♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 8, final system: pp run, Meno mosso, held bass, ritardando and the final chord.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Composer’s arrangement for piano (1911) of Franz Behr’s Scherzpolka Lachtäubchen, Op. 303, as played by him
fields.note: The printed title is Polka de W. R. (W. for Wassily, the composer’s father); the RCA set and the Archive file use V.R. Behr’s theme is transposed from F to A♭ with an added counter-melody and without Behr’s middle section. The score prints ossia alternatives, and the edition used by the composer for this recording is not identified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82187 (10-inch double-faced; Polka on side L, Prelude in C♯ minor on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Florida Atlantic catalogue; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by the National Park Service and Densmore (December 1920) and is not followed for the release date; either proposed publication year predates 1926.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The RCA register names Edison 6744-B for CD 10, track 15, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition. Franz Behr died in 1898, so the underlying polka is also out of copyright on the same calculation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82187, released December 1920).
fields.note: The National Park Service catalogue and Densmore’s list both give a December 1920 release for Edison 82187, whose side L carries the Polka; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
